questions.topic: Selective use of evidence
questions.learningObjective: Identify quoted figures that leave out the countervailing evidence

He has quoted the wrong month, since only the previous quarter may be used to compare branches fairly
options.misconception: believes the fault is the choice of month rather than the omission of other branches

options.text: He has misread the delay figures, since branch delay minutes are always higher than main line minutes
options.misconception: assumes branch figures must be wrong rather than selectively reported

options.text: Nothing is wrong with the entry, since a daily log naturally records the figures the dispatcher works with
options.misconception: treats a working log as exempt from showing all the relevant evidence

questions.explanation: Selecting the branch with the worst figures and saying nothing about the others is quoting selectively. The claim about the region can only be assessed if the branches left out are named.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A term carrying two senses across a passage
questions.learningObjective: Determine which sense of a term a passage is using

stimulus.body: A dispatcher writes that the 18:04 was terminated after a four minute delay. The same entry notes that the unit worked the service through to the terminus after the delay was cleared.

questions.stem: A colleague reads terminated as meaning the service was cancelled before departure. Why is that reading wrong?

options.text: It means the service was cancelled, since controllers use the word for any disruption to a booked path
options.misconception: assumes a single technical term has one fixed sense in every entry

options.text: In this entry the word means the service stopped short of its destination, since it resumed after the delay
It means the service was withdrawn for the day, since terminated runs never restart their journey
options.misconception: confuses a temporary hold with permanent withdrawal of the service

options.text: It means the service ran past its normal destination, since the word describes what happened after the delay
options.misconception: reads a temporary finish as an extension beyond the normal route

questions.explanation: The entry records the service resuming after the delay, so terminated there marks an early finish rather than a cancellation. A word can carry different senses across a passage, and the surrounding facts fix which sense applies.
questions.hint: Ask what the entry says happened to the service afterwards.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Who must show what
questions.learningObjective: Explain how possession of evidence determines who must produce a case
questions.stem: A controller is asked to justify a delay in the log but says the burden lies with the passenger who complained. Explain who must show what.

answer.exemplar: The controller is the one who holds the operational record, so the duty to produce the reason for the delay sits with the controller and the company, not with the passenger who reported it. A complainant supplies the occasion for scrutiny but has no access to the running data, the signal logs or the crew records that would settle the question. Putting the evidential burden on the passenger would mean the delay could go unexplained simply because one passenger did not gather and present records that already exist.

questions.explanation: Whoever holds the evidence must produce it, and here that is the controller and the operator. The passenger triggering the complaint has neither the records nor the standing to explain the delay.
questions.hint: Ask who holds the records that would settle the point.

questions.stem: A log entry explains a missed path by saying the driver was running late, with nothing further. Which judgement is fairest?

options.text: The entry is acceptable, since a driver's lateness is a matter for the driver and the roster office
options.misconception: treats a bare attribution to a person as an adequate explanation

options.text: The entry should be withdrawn, because entries naming individuals are never appropriate in an operational log
options.misconception: rules out any mention of an individual as though it were improper

options.text: The entry should state the facts behind the lateness and the action taken, so the entry can be checked and used
The entry should be rewritten to mention the other drivers involved, so the pattern becomes visible
options.misconception: asks for a broader blame rather than a repairable explanation

questions.explanation: Naming a person is not naming a cause: the reader cannot check the entry or act on it. The repair is to record the observable facts behind the delay and what was done about it.
questions.hint: Ask what facts the reader would need in order to act.

questions.stem: Which adjustment would make this summary strongest as an argument?

options.text: Replace the summary with the raw log extracts, so the reader can see the figures without an argument
options.misconception: believes evidence alone substitutes for a structured argument

options.text: Set out the claim first, then present the evidence in the order that builds it, ending with the request
Add the total cost of the work at the end, since cost is what decides such questions

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Selective use of evidence
questions.learningObjective: Explain how to correct a summary built on one-sided figures
questions.stem: A report lists three late trains and one early train from the same week, then says the service is unreliable. Explain the fault and how to correct it.

answer.exemplar: The report quotes only the late workings and passes over the early one, so the figures show the dispatcher's worst cases rather than the service's typical performance. The correction is to state the rule used for selection and then show the full picture for the same period, including the early and the punctual workings, so that a reader can judge the rate rather than the anecdotes that happened to be noticed.

questions.explanation: Quoting three late workings and omitting the early one is selection, not evidence, because the omitted case bears directly on the claim. The report should state its selection rule and show the full week.
questions.hint: Ask what the fourth working shows about the pattern.

questions.learningObjective: Spot a cause credited with an effect that came before it

questions.stem: What is the main fault in the notice's reasoning?

options.misconception: treats imprecision of dating as though it voided the reasoning

options.text: It relies on a single junction, so no general claim could ever be drawn from one place
options.misconception: raises a scope objection where the ordering of events is the real fault

options.text: It should name the engineers who signed off the work, so the responsibility is traceable

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Statements that can be argued about
questions.learningObjective: Explain what makes a causal statement in a log arguable
questions.stem: A log entry states that the 14:32 was held for 11 minutes because the route was congested. Explain whether this can be argued about and what would help.

answer.exemplar: The statement can be argued about, because it makes a claim about the world rather than recording a preference: the hold is a measured figure and the congestion is a proposed cause that can be checked. To argue it well, the entry should say which part of the route was congested, at what time, and what the corridor normally runs like, since without that the reader can neither confirm the cause nor offer an alternative such as a late inbound unit occupying the platform.

questions.explanation: It asserts a measurable hold and a cause, and both can be contested with evidence about the route and the time. Vague causal wording is arguable rather than immune from argument.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader would need in order to disagree.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Naming a fault and repairing it
questions.learningObjective: Explain what an entry must contain if it is to prevent a repeat
questions.stem: A controller's note says the plan was 'not followed properly'. Explain the problem with the entry and how to correct it.

answer.exemplar: The phrase identifies no action, no person and no point in the plan, so a reader cannot tell what went wrong, cannot check the account against the records and cannot learn anything that would stop a repeat. The entry should name the plan, the instruction that was not carried out, the instruction that should have been followed, and any factor that made the instruction difficult to see, since that last part is what turns a fault into something that can be designed out.

questions.explanation: Naming a fault means naming the action that was wrong and the action that was needed. Without both, the entry records a mood rather than an event and offers nothing for prevention.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader must do differently next time.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Who must show what
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a duty to produce evidence follows from who holds the records
questions.stem: An inquiry asks why a service was cancelled. Explain who must show what and why the allocation follows from that.

answer.exemplar: The duty to produce the reasons sits with the operator, since it alone holds the timetable, the crew roster, the fault log and the record of what the controller decided at the time. Once those are produced, the inquiry can test one explanation against another: a shortage of drivers, a failed train that blocked the platform, or a late running service that required the turn to be short-worked. The passenger who gave notice of the cancellation can confirm that it happened and roughly when, but cannot be expected to establish the operational reason for it.

questions.explanation: The party holding the records must produce them, and only the operator holds the fault log, roster and control decisions. The allocation follows from where the evidence is, not from who complained.
questions.hint: Ask which records exist and who keeps them.

The note should have included the passenger counts for the previous March, so a comparison could be made
options.misconception: asks for a baseline rather than addressing the rival explanation

options.text: The note should have quoted the passengers who found the timetable convenient, since they are the evidence
options.misconception: seeks anecdotal support for a causal claim that needs rivals excluded

options.text: The note should have been written by the commercial team rather than by operations, since it concerns demand
options.misconception: redirects the fault to authorship rather than to the reasoning

questions.explanation: The note offers one cause while a second change on the same dates could produce the same crowding, and it never rules that out. The explanation has to survive the rival account before it can stand.
questions.hint: Ask what else changed on those dates.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Selective use of evidence
questions.learningObjective: Explain why internal figures cannot establish a comparative ranking
questions.stem: A report claims a service is the most reliable in the district using its own punctuality figures alone. Explain the fault and how to fix it.

answer.exemplar: The figures quoted are the operator's own, and the report never compares them with the figures of the other operators in the district, so a high internal percentage says nothing about how the service stands against the alternatives a passenger actually has. The fix is to set out the comparison across operators for the same period and the same measure, to say how each operator defines punctuality, and to note where the definitions differ, since that difference alone can move a service several places in the ranking.

questions.explanation: A service cannot be called the most reliable in a district on the strength of its own numbers alone, because the comparison has been left out. The report needs other operators' figures for the same period and measure.
questions.hint: Ask whose figures would have to be added to test the claim.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Statements that can be argued about
questions.learningObjective: Propose a testable comparison behind a comparative judgement
questions.stem: A supervisor says the 06:12 is 'the most difficult path in the area'. How can this be tested?

options.text: By asking other supervisors whether they agree, since experienced judgement settles such questions
options.misconception: substitutes consensus of opinion for a checkable comparison

options.text: By comparing how often the path is granted and how much slack it leaves against nearby paths
By looking at whether the path is scheduled at the busiest time, since difficulty is a scheduling matter
options.misconception: confuses when a path is used with how hard it is to work

options.text: It cannot be tested, since difficulty is a matter of judgement and judgements resist measurement
options.misconception: treats a comparison of the kind the sentence makes as beyond testing

questions.explanation: The claim compares paths, and comparisons of this kind can be tested against granting rates and against the slack each path allows. That a sentence expresses judgement does not make it untestable.
questions.hint: Ask what the sentence is comparing the path with.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Sequence for building a sourced argument
questions.learningObjective: Order the parts of a board case so the need precedes the request
questions.stem: First, identify what the board is being asked to accept. Then choose the arrangement that makes the case.

options.text: The recommendation, the evidence for it and the reasons for rejecting the other options
options.misconception: leads with the request and treats the need as given

options.text: The evidence, the options and the recommendation, so the board sees the material before the ask
options.misconception: supplies evidence before there is a claim for it to serve

options.text: The cost, the benefit and the recommendation, since a board decides on figures and nothing else
options.misconception: assumes a board decides on figures alone, ignoring the need

options.text: The need for change, the evidence for it, the options considered and the reasons for the recommendation

questions.explanation: The board is being asked to accept a need, and the evidence has to establish that need before the options and the recommendation make sense. An order that starts anywhere else leaves the request unsupported.
questions.hint: Ask what has to be accepted before the request means anything.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Selective use of evidence
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a summary of exceptions describes nothing typical
questions.stem: A controller's monthly summary lists the services that were late and none of the services that were on time. What follows?

options.text: The summary cannot support a claim about the typical service, since the data it prints are the exception cases
The summary is complete, because every service that ran is recorded somewhere in the monthly book
options.misconception: assumes a complete underlying record makes a selective summary complete

options.text: The summary should be headed 'late services' so the reader knows it is not a record of all services
options.misconception: thinks a better label repairs the omission of the punctual services

options.text: The summary should give the delay minutes for each service listed, so the scale of the lateness is visible
options.misconception: asks for more precision where the real problem is the selection

questions.explanation: Printing only the late services gives a reader the exceptions and none of the ordinary cases, so nothing about the typical service can be drawn from it. The selection has to be reversed or declared.
questions.hint: Ask what the unlisted services would show.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Who must show what
questions.learningObjective: Resolve a dispute by assigning the duty to produce the records

stimulus.body: A passenger disputes that the train was held for a signal failure, saying the train was late because it waited for a late inbound service. The company says the log records the signal failure and the driver says she saw the inbound arrive late first.

questions.stem: Who must show what to resolve this dispute?

options.text: The passenger must show it, since she is the one making the claim that the signal was at fault
options.misconception: puts the burden on the person asserting the alternative account

options.text: The company must produce the control log and timing records, since it holds them and the passenger holds neither
The driver must show it, since she was present and the company has no account of the platform
options.misconception: assumes the employer holds nothing, ignoring the control log

options.text: Both must show it equally, since neither account can be preferred without the other's records
options.misconception: makes the burden mutual and leaves the records with nobody

questions.explanation: The passenger has raised a competing account but holds no operational records, while the company holds the log and the timings. The party in possession of the evidence must produce it for the dispute to be settled.
questions.hint: Ask who holds the timing records for that hour.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A conclusion already assumed
questions.learningObjective: Explain an assumption in which cause and effect may run the other way
questions.stem: A note argues that the service should be shortened because the branch is underused. Explain the assumption and how to remove it.

answer.exemplar: The note has assumed that the service is not running because the branch is underused, when the direction of the reasoning may be the other way round: a short working reduces what passengers can do, and the underuse may be a consequence of the service rather than a cause for ending it. The note should state what the service currently offers, look at the demand that exists for journeys the service cannot make, and compare the usage of comparable branches that run a fuller service before it uses underuse as a reason to reduce what is offered.

questions.explanation: Underuse and a reduced service can each cause the other, so the note has used one to justify the other without asking which came first. The demand the service cannot currently meet has to be examined.
questions.hint: Ask which way round the causes might run.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Sequence for building a sourced argument
questions.learningObjective: Sequence the parts of a report so each piece does work for the next
questions.stem: A report argues that a junction should be upgraded. Which arrangement of the material serves the argument best?

options.text: The option proposed, the cost of the alternatives, and the records that show the consequences
options.misconception: leads with the proposal so the reader has no need to be convinced

options.text: The records, the cost of the alternatives and the option proposed, so every fact is on the table
options.misconception: supplies facts in an order that leaves the need unestablished

options.text: The consequences of the present layout, the records that show them, the alternatives tried and the option proposed
The consequences of the present layout, the option proposed and the records that show the consequences
options.misconception: puts the records after the proposal so they read as decoration

questions.explanation: The argument works when the present consequences are established by the records, the alternatives are shown to have been tried and the proposal follows as the response. Moving any part breaks the chain.
questions.hint: Ask whether each piece is doing work for the piece after it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A term carrying two senses across a passage
questions.learningObjective: Locate the shift of sense and apply the second sense correctly
questions.stem: First, mark the shift of sense in the passage. Then choose the reading that follows from it.

options.text: In the second entry the word means the people who work the route rather than the service itself
In the second entry the word means the service itself rather than the people who work the route
options.misconception: reverses the two senses the passage distinguishes

options.text: In both entries the word means the service, so the passage uses it in a single consistent sense
options.misconception: ignores the clear shift between the two entries

options.text: In the first entry the word means the people who work the route rather than the service itself
options.misconception: locates the shift in the wrong entry

questions.explanation: The passage contrasts the staff with the service in the second entry, so the sense there shifts from the service to those who run it. Misplacing the shift or treating the passage as uniform both misread it.
questions.hint: Ask what the second entry contrasts with what.
